case_name: Kalo v. The Law Society of Manitoba
text:
Date:  20140131

Docket: CI 13-01-84092

(Winnipeg Centre)

Indexed as: Kalo v. The
Law Society of Manitoba

Cited as:  2014 MBQB 24

COURT OF QUEEN’S BENCH
OF MANITOBA

B E T W E E N:

MICHAEL KALO,

)

In person

)

applicant,

)

)

- and -

)

)

THE LAW SOCIETY OF MANITOBA,

)

Leah Kosokowsky

)

for the respondent

)

respondent.

)

)

)

JUDGMENT DELIVERED:

)

January 31, 2014

MASTER COOPER

[
1
]

This is a motion for security for costs brought by the respondent, The
Law Society of Manitoba (“the Law Society”), on an application by Michael Kalo for judicial review of a decision
of an appeal panel of the Law Society. The appeal
panel upheld the decision of the Director of Admissions and Membership of the Law Society to deny
Mr. Kalo admission to the Law Society as an articling student and to the CPLED (Canadian Centre for
Professional Legal Education) bar admission program.

[
2
]

Queen’s Bench Rule 56.01 gives the court the
discretion to order security for costs where it is just in the circumstances of the
case. It sets out some circumstances where it may be appropriate, including where a plaintiff has failed to pay costs
ordered in the same or another proceeding.

56.01 The court, on motion in a proceeding may make
such order for security for costs as in the particular circumstances of the
case is just, including where the plaintiff or applicant,

(a)  is ordinarily resident outside Manitoba;

(b)  has another proceeding for the same relief
pending;

(c)  has failed to pay costs as ordered in the
same or another proceeding;

(d)  is a corporation or a nominal plaintiff, and
there is good reason to believe that insufficient assets will be available in
Manitoba to pay costs, if ordered to do so; or

(e)  a statute requires security for costs.

[
3
]

The Law Society asserts that Mr. Kalo has
failed to pay costs in other proceedings and, for this
and other reasons, it is just that security for costs
be ordered.  Mr. Kalo does not concede that costs
orders to the Law Society are outstanding: he argues that his intervening
bankruptcy must be considered.  He submits that he is impecunious and for that
and other reasons an order for security for costs would be unjust.

Failure to Pay Costs

[
4
]

There is no question that Mr. Kalo has failed
to pay costs as ordered in other proceedings, including other proceedings
related to his efforts to be
admitted to the bar admission program.   Indeed Mr. Kalo has been involved in a
multitude of proceedings over the last several years, has been ordered to pay
costs on numerous occasions,  and
has not paid them.

[
5
]

In his family proceedings, Justice Allen ordered him to pay over
$126,000.00 in costs (FD03-01-69719).  On June 12, 2009, Thomson J. ordered Mr.
Kalo to pay security for costs of $1000.00 in relation to his pending motion to
vary Justice Allen’s order. In his judgment,
Shore-Kalo v. Kalo
,

2009 MBQB 168
, [2009] M.J. No. 241 (QL), he considered Mr. Kalo’s impecuniosity,
the unpaid costs orders against him, the multiplicity of court proceedings
initiated by him and his inappropriate conduct, and the marginal merit of this
motion. Mr. Kalo’s appeal of this decision was dismissed with costs in
Shore-Kalo
v. Kalo
,
2009 MBCA 104
, [2009] M.J. No. 352 (QL).  Presumably the costs
made against him in his family proceedings were part, if not all, of the $140,000.00 he
declared to be owing to his former wife in his statement of affairs when he made an assignment into bankruptcy on October 28, 2009 (see BK13-01-02984).

[
6
]

Mr. Kalo has instituted many other actions. Two applications were filed in 2006 asking to have him declared a
vexatious litigant under s. 73(1) of
The Court of
Queen’s Bench Act
(CI06-01-49383 and CI06-01-49450).  These ended in
consent orders dated December 19, 2006, which
essentially involved an admission by Mr. Kalo that he was a vexatious litigant.
Specifically, they provided that Mr. Kalo was
prohibited from instituting
any legal proceedings against a number of named parties and others, without leave of a
judge, until his youngest child is eighteen, and that certain outstanding costs orders that had
been obtained against Mr. Kalo would not be pursued.

Failure to Pay Costs to the Law Society

•

First application for admission

[
7
]

In October 2008, Mr. Kalo applied to the Law
Society for admission as an articling student and for admission to the Manitoba
bar admission program.

[
8
]

On November 17, 2008, while the Law Society was
investigating his character and fitness to be admitted, Mr. Kalo applied to the
court for interim and permanent declaratory orders on an urgent basis in
relation to the investigation and his application for admission  (QB file No.
CI08-01-58970). The Law Society moved for security for costs and, on December
10, 2008,   the late Scurfield J. ordered Mr. Kalo to post security for costs
in the amount of $3500.00 before proceeding with his application.  Mr. Kalo did
not pay these costs and filed a notice of abandonment of the application on
October 13, 2009.  Although no reasons were issued by the court, it is perhaps
worth noting that Mr. Kalo’s defence to the motion included an assertion of
impecuniosity.

[
9
]

The investigation was still pending, when on
May 4, 2009, Mr. Kalo filed an application in the court (CI09-01-61085) against
the Law Society, the CEO of the Law Society and Joe Gallagher, the
investigator, seeking an order that the Chief Executive Officer of the Law
Society not have any input into the investigation on the grounds of bias or apprehension of bias,
that the investigation be “deemed complete without any findings” against him,
or, in the alternative, orders requiring the Law Society to approve his
application or to complete the investigation by June 1, 2009. He abandoned this
application by notice filed October 13, 2009.

[
10
]

In August 2009, after completion of the
investigation, the Director of Admissions and Membership denied his application
on the grounds that he was not of good moral character or a fit and proper
person to be admitted.  Mr. Kalo appealed that decision and requested that he
be permitted to begin the CPLED program while his appeal was proceeding. The
Director also denied that request, and Mr. Kalo appealed that decision.

[
11
]

A panel of the Admissions and Education
Committee of the Law Society conducted a hearing on August 26 and 27, 2009,
and, in a decision dated September 2, 2009, concluded that he was not of good
moral character or a fit and proper person to be admitted.  The panel indicated
that it would be providing full reasons later.

[
12
]

On September 8, 2009, before the panel’s full
reasons were delivered, Mr. Kalo appealed to the Court of Appeal, and filed a
motion for an order on short leave directing the Law Society to admit him to
the 2009-2010 CPLED program pending completion of the court proceedings on the
appeal (AI09-30-07228).  By
written decision dated September 29, 2009, Monnin J.A. dismissed the motion on
the basis of no jurisdiction and awarded costs to the Law Society of $350.00 as
requested by the Law Society.

[
13
]

The first appeal panel issued its reasons for
decision on October 9, 2009, in which they dismissed both of Mr. Kalo’s
appeals.

[
14
]

On October 16, 2009, Mr. Kalo filed an
application for judicial review of this decision (CI09-01-63339). Martin J. dismissed his application for
judicial review in an oral decision on January 7, 2010 and ordered costs to the
Law Society, later set at $3,069.12.

[
15
]

On January 11, 2010, Mr. Kalo filed an appeal
of Justice Martin’s decision  and a few days later, by letter dated January 15,
2010, he wrote to the Registrar of the Court of Appeal asking that his appeal
be scheduled for a hearing “without any further delays”. The Registrar advised
him that he would need to file a signed copy of Justice Martin’s order as well
as a transcript of his reasons before the date could be set.

[
16
]

Mr. Kalo then filed a motion with the Court of
Appeal on January 21, 2010, asking for short leave and an order directing the
registrar “to immediately set
an early
date for the hearing”.  On
January 27, 2010, the Law Society filed a motion for short leave and security
for costs. On January 28, 2010, Beard J.A. dismissed Mr. Kalo’s motion and
awarded costs of $200.00 to the Law Society.  She adjourned the security for
costs motion to March 4, 2010, at which time it was heard by Chartier J.A., as he then was.  By written decision
dated March 8, 2010, he granted the Law Society’s motion,  ordered that Mr. Kalo post security of
$1000.00 within 120 days, and
awarded the Law Society costs, later set at $486.38.  Mr. Kalo immediately
appealed this order.  The appeal was scheduled to be heard on May 31, 2010.

[
17
]

On May 7, 2010, Mr. Kalo by letter requested
that his appeal be adjourned until after the summer recess for reasons which
included a planned trip to Israel, and a possible appeal of Legal Aid
Manitoba’s denial of his application.   He was advised he needed to file a
motion which he did on May 17, 2010.

[
18
]

On May 31, 2010, a panel of the Court of Appeal
dismissed Mr. Kalo’s request for an adjournment and his appeal of the order for
security for costs. The court ordered he pay costs of $350.00 on his motion to
adjourn and $2000.00 on the appeal. Mr. Kalo did not post the security, nor pay
any of the costs ordered , and he did not proceed with his appeal.

•

Second Application for Admission

[
19
]

On April 5, 2010, while his appeal of the
first rejection was pending, Mr. Kalo submitted his second application for
admission to the CPLED program.

[
20
]

By letter dated June 10, 2010, the Director of
Admissions denied his second application on the grounds he was not of good moral character or a fit and
proper person to be admitted.  On June 11, 2010, Mr. Kalo appealed the
Director’s decision.  Mr. Kalo
filed six preliminary motions, including a motion that
the chair of the panel recuse himself, and a seventh
motion in the course of the hearing, all of which were
dismissed.

[
21
]

The second appeal panel dismissed his appeal in a written decision
dated November 25, 2010.  A rule enacted by the Law Society in April 2010 would
require an unsuccessful applicant to wait two years before applying again.
This time could be abridged by the Law Society if the applicant could
demonstrate a material change in circumstances. On April 14, 2011, Mr. Kalo
applied to abridge the two year waiting period, and on May 17, 2011, the
Director of Admissions denied his request on the basis that there was no
material change in circumstances.  He appealed this decision on May 30, 2011,
and on July 6, 2011, the Chairperson of the Admissions and Education Committee
of the Law Society dismissed his appeal.

•

Third application for admission

[
22
]

Mr. Kalo submitted this third application for
admission as an articling student on September 24, 2012.  The Director of Admissions
denied this application on
November 1, 2012, again on the grounds that he was neither of good moral
character nor a fit and proper person to be admitted.  Mr. Kalo appealed this
decision on December 3, 2012, and a third hearing panel dismissed his appeal by
written decision dated April 25, 2013. The panel
concluded that he had not established that he was now of good character and
fitness.

[
23
]

Mr. Kalo applied for judicial review of the
third panel’s decision on June 19, 2013. This is the application in which this
motion for security for costs is brought.
Specifically, in his application he is seeking, an order quashing the panel’s
decision and an order directing the Law Society to promptly and unconditionally
enrol him in the Manitoba CPLED program and register him as an articling
student,
inter alia
.

[
24
]

The motion was first returnable on the judges’
list on July 17, 2013. Suche J. ordered that the matter be adjourned to August
16, 2013 before a master. She further ordered that, subject to any order made
on the respondent’s motion for security for costs extending the time, the
respondent would have seven days in which to file material in response to the
application, which period was to run from the later of the date on which the
appeal period from the decision of the master expired or from the final
determination of the motion for security for costs.

[
25
]

The parties attended before me on August 16,
2013.  Mr. Kalo made an oral motion at the commencement of the hearing requesting
that I recuse myself from hearing the security for costs motion on the grounds
of reasonable apprehension of bias.

[
26
]

In the particular circumstances, including the
fact that counsel for the Law Society, Leah Kosokowsky, indicated she was
ready to proceed, I allowed Mr.
Kalo to proceed with his oral motion.

What
follows in the next paragraphs is basically summarized or extracted from the
written reasons for decision delivered on September 10, 2013.

[
27
]

The applicant’s position, as expressed at the
hearing, was that I should
recuse myself because of a statement I made in a report that I wrote in 2008 on an accounting under
The Family
Property Act
,
Shore-Kalo v. Kalo
,
2008 MBQB 134
, [2008] M.J.
No. 220, (QL), part of which was quoted in an affidavit filed by the Law
Society in support of this motion. This affidavit, affirmed by Allan Fineblit, Q.C., Chief Executive
Officer of the Law Society, is basically a summary of the various legal
proceedings brought by the applicant in relation to his quest to be admitted to
the bar admission course, including
particulars as to the cost orders made against the respondent and his payment
history in relation to them. The affidavit also refers to other legal
proceedings involving the applicant, including the applicant’s bankruptcy and
family proceedings.

[
28
]

In paragraph 41 of his affidavit, Mr. Fineblit
alleges:

Based on a review of some judicial decisions involving
Kalo, I am concerned that he has no concern for cost consequences that may be
imposed upon him by the Courts.  For example, in reading a decision of Master
Joy Cooper in suit No. FD 03-01-69719 confirmed on June 12, 2008, she commented
at paragraph 73 that:
[Mr. Kalo] seems to be impervious to cost orders and
indeed indicated to me in the hearing on December 19, 2007 that the bigger the
costs, the bigger the bankruptcy
.”

[
29
]

Counsel for the Law Society presented a number of authorities in support of the Law Society’s
position that there was no basis for me to recuse myself. The applicant did not
question any of this authority nor present any case law to the contrary.  I commented in my decision as follows:

A claim of reasonable apprehension of bias is a very
serious one.  As the Supreme Court of Canada stated in
Wewaykum Indian
Band v. Canada
,
2003 SCC 45
,
[2003] 2 S.C.R. 259 (QL)
:

2        An allegation that a judgment may be tainted
by bias or by a reasonable apprehension of bias is most serious. That
allegation calls into question the impartiality of the Court and its members
and raises doubt on the public's perception of the Court's ability to render
justice according to law.

The impartiality of judges is a keystone of our legal
system.  There is a presumption of impartiality and the onus is on the party
seeking disqualification to establish circumstances that justify
disqualification.  In the same decision, the court commented:

57
…(P)ublic confidence in our
legal system is rooted in the fundamental belief that those who adjudicate
[page288] in law must always do so without bias or prejudice and must be
perceived to do so.

58
The essence of impartiality
lies in the requirement of the judge to approach the case to be adjudicated
with an open mind. Conversely, bias or prejudice has been defined as

a leaning, inclination, bent or predisposition towards
one side or another or a particular result. In its application to legal
proceedings, it represents a predisposition to decide an issue or cause in a
certain way which does not leave the judicial mind perfectly open to
conviction. Bias is a condition or state of mind which sways judgment and renders
a judicial officer unable to exercise his or her functions impartially in a
particular case.

(
R. v. Bertram
,
[1989] O.J. No. 2123
(QL)
(H.C.)
, quoted by Cory
J. in
R. v. S. (R.D
.)
,
1997 CanLII 324 (SCC)
,
[1997] 3 S.C.R. 484
, at para.
106
.)

59
Viewed in this light,
"[i]mpartiality is the fundamental qualification of a judge and the core
attribute of the judiciary" (Canadian Judicial Council,
Ethical
Principles for Judges
(1998), at p. 30). It is the key to our judicial
process, and must be presumed. As was noted by L'Heureux-Dubé J. and McLachlin
J. (as she then was)
in
S. (R.D.)
, supra
, at para.
32
, the presumption
of impartiality carries considerable weight, and the law should not carelessly
evoke the possibility of bias in a judge, whose authority depends upon that
presumption. Thus, while the requirement of judicial impartiality is a
stringent one, the burden is on the party arguing for disqualification to
establish that the circumstances justify a finding that the judge must be
disqualified.

The court observed that the apprehension of bias must
be a reasonable one, held by reasonable and right-minded persons, applying
themselves to the question and obtaining the required information:

60
In Canadian law, one standard
has now emerged as the criterion for disqualification. The criterion, as
expressed by de Grandpré J. in
Committee for Justice and Liberty v. National
Energy Board, supra
, at p. 394, is the reasonable apprehension of bias:

[page289]

... the apprehension of bias must be a reasonable one,
held by reasonable and right minded persons, applying themselves to the
question and obtaining thereon the required information. In the words of the
Court of Appeal, that test is "what would an informed person, viewing the
matter realistically and practically -- and having thought the matter through
-- conclude. Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the
decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide
fairly."

In
Kalo v. Manitoba (Human Rights Commission
)
,
Joyal J., as he then was, commented that the law in Canada requires the
objecting party to demonstrate a real likelihood or probability of bias and a
“mere suspicion”  is not enough:

18

That test had been previously reaffirmed
in

R. v.

S.(R.D.)
,

1997 CanLII 324 (SCC)
,
[1997] 3 S.C.R. 484
,

[1997] S.C.J. No. 84

(QL)
. In that case, the
Supreme Court of Canada confirmed at para. 112 that Canadian law also requires
that a real likelihood or probability of bias must be demonstrated and that a
"mere suspicion" is not enough. Additionally, the reasonable person,
about whom reference is made in the governing test, must be
"informed". That is, a reasonable person must be informed not only of
the relevant circumstances of the particular case, but also of the tradition of
integrity and impartiality that are the backdrop for our judicial system and
which are reflected in and reinforced by the judicial oath. In

R. v.

S.(R.D.), supra
, Cory J. stated:

para. 116 Often the most significant occasion in the
career of a judge is the swearing of the oath of office. It is a moment of
pride and joy coupled with a realization of the onerous responsibility that
goes with the office. The taking of the oath is solemn and a defining moment
etched forever in the memory of the judge. The oath requires a judge to render
justice impartially. To take that oath is the fulfilment of a life's dreams. It
is never taken lightly. Throughout their careers, Canadian judges strive to
overcome the personal biases that are common to all humanity in order to
provide and clearly appear to provide a fair trial for all who come before
them. Their rate of success in this difficult endeavour is high.

19

On
an application which alleges a reasonable apprehension of bias based upon prior
judicial involvement, the applicant must satisfy the impugned judge that a
reasonable, right-minded and properly informed person, viewing the matter
realistically and practically, would view the impugned judge's involvement as
consciously or unconsciously biased as a result of the prior participation in
the other matters involving the applicant. "Bias" in such
circumstances means a predisposition to decide the issues in a way which would
suggest that the judge's mind was not completely open.
See

Wewaykum
Indian Band
, supra

at para.
58
.

20

As
there is a strong presumption in favour of judicial impartiality, the alleged
grounds advanced to support recusal must be serious and convincing.
In

Wewaykum Indian Band
, the Supreme Court of Canada stated:

para. 59 ... [W]hile the requirement of judicial
impartiality is a stringent one, the burden is on the party arguing for
disqualification to establish that the circumstances justify a finding that the
judge must be disqualified.

23

Although
justice must be seen to be done, it is equally important that judicial officers
discharge their duty to sit and that they not too readily or scrupulously cede
to unjustifiable suggestions respecting the appearance of bias.

24

In

Committee for Justice and Liberty et al.
v.

National
Energy Board et al.
,

1976 CanLII 2 (SCC)
,
[1978] 1 S.C.R. 369

at 395,

[1976] S.C.J. No. 118

(QL)
, de Grandpré J. discussed the reasonable apprehension
standard with the accompanying reminder:

... The grounds for this apprehension must, however,
be

substantial

and
I entirely agree with the Federal Court of Appeal which refused to accept the suggestion
that the test be related to the "very sensitive or scrupulous
conscience".

The recusal motion is based on the sole allegation
that in the family property proceeding I made a reference to the applicant’s
seeming imperviousness respecting costs and referred to comments he had made in
the proceeding.  There are no other allegations or evidence of bias whatsoever.
There is no evidence apart from this that could suggest any kind of
predisposition against him in this proceeding, and this evidence does not
demonstrate that I would be predisposed against the applicant or treat him in
any way unfairly.

The law is clear that the mere fact that a judge has
made negative findings in another proceeding does not in itself raise a
reasonable apprehension of bias.  As Joyal C.J.Q.B. stated in
Kalo v
Human Rights Commission
:

21     As the
court noted in that case, there are no "textbook" cases of bias and
in each case, the inquiry is highly fact-specific:

para. 77 ... Whether the facts, as
established, point to financial or personal interest of the decision-maker;
present or past link with a party, counsel or judge; earlier participation or
knowledge of the litigation; or expression of views and activities, they must
be addressed carefully in light of the entire context.
There are no
shortcuts.
[emphasis added]

22

One
of the shortcuts that the courts have identified and rejected is that shortcut
which flows from the proposition that apprehended bias will inexorably follow
from a judge's prior involvement in proceedings involving the same litigant.
In

R. v.

Werner
,

2005 NWTCA 5
,

205 C.C.C. (3d) 556
, the Northwest Territories Court of
Appeal stated:

para. 18 As many cases have noted, therefore, the mere
fact that a judge had previously decided adversely a case involving an accused
does not create a reasonable apprehension of bias: see
, for example,

R. v.

Novak
,

1995 CanLII 2024 (BC CA)
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 1127

(QL)
,

27 W.C.B. (2d) 295
(C.A.)
;

R. v.

Teskey
,

[1995] A.J. No. þþ311

(QL),

26 W.C.B. (2d) 550

(Q.B.)
;

R. v.

James

(2000),
2000 BCCA 616 (CanLII)
,
149 C.C.C. (3d) 534

...;

R. v.

Kochan
,
2001 ABQB 346 (CanLII)
,
[2001] A.J. No. 555

(QL)
,

50 W.C.B. (2d) 18

(Q.B.)
. The presumption of judicial
impartiality prevails in the absence of cogent evidence to the contrary.

See also

West v.

Wilbur
,

2002 NBQB 376 (CanLII)
,
[2002] N.B.J. No. 430

(C.A.)
(QL)
;

R. v.

Tremblay
,

2004 ABCA 102
,

[2004] A.J. No. 323

(C.A.)
(QL)
.

The fact that the impugned comments relate to a matter
at issue in the motion for security for costs- the likelihood the applicant
would satisfy a costs order - does not alter the situation because of the
context in which those comments were made.  The comments were made in the
context of that particular proceeding and there is no evidence otherwise
.

[
30
]

I concluded that Mr. Kalo had failed to
meet his onus to establish a reasonable apprehension of bias as the fact that in previous proceedings I had made a negative observation regarding
his conduct in relation to costs was no impediment to my hearing the Law Society’s motion for security
for costs. I accordingly dismissed his motion.

[
31
]

I did not make an award of costs at that time,
assuming the parties could agree on costs, and if not, I invited them to make
an appointment to speak to it.  They did not agree, and a hearing was held on
October 2, 2013. The Law Society requested costs of only $500.00 inclusive, an
amount considerably less than tariff, taking into account the circumstances.  I
ordered the amount requested by the Law Society, payable in any event of the
cause. I did not order them to be paid forthwith, only because in my view that
would go to the heart of the motion for security for costs yet to be heard and
decided by me.

[
32
]

The parties were unable to agree on a date for
the hearing of the motion, and appeared before Master Berthaudin on the
masters’ uncontested list on October 8, 2013. They had been offered two dates,
October 17 and November 21, but counsel for the Law Society was unavailable on
October 17. Mr. Kalo wanted the earlier date. Master Berthaudin set the matter
to be heard on November 21, 2013.

[
33
]

The very next day, Mr. Kalo sent a letter to me
asking for an appointment with me after trying to file a requisition with the
Master’s Co-ordinator to set his application before me on the uncontested list
on which I was presiding on October 16, 2013.  Mr. Kalo was seeking an earlier
date for the hearing of the motion, either by my “making time” for it, or by my
referring it to another master or a judge or without conducting an oral hearing
or that, at the very least, I start the hearing earlier than the time set by
Master Berthaudin.

[
34
]

I replied that it would be inappropriate to for
me to revisit the hearing date as it was set by Master Berthaudin after hearing
from both Mr. Kalo and Ms Kosokowsky.  I was eventually able to determine that
I could start the hearing earlier in the afternoon to convenience Mr. Kalo.

Outstanding Court Costs Payable to the Law
Society

[
35
]

In summary, the court
has ordered Mr. Kalo to pay costs totaling $6,455.50 to the Law Society in other proceedings.  The costs he was ordered
to pay after his assignment into bankruptcy on October 28, 2009 total
$6,105.50.  He has not made any payments on these outstanding costs. Together with my order as to costs in the amount of $500.00, the
total owing to the Law Society is $6,605.50.

[
36
]

In his motion brief, Mr.
Kalo submitted that because
the costs in the other proceedings were ordered after his assignment in bankruptcy and before his
automatic discharge received on July 29, 2010: “Even by the Official Receiver these costs
might anyhow have been included” in his opposed bankruptcy.  He says correspondence from Scott Armstrong, Senior Debtor
Compliance Bankruptcy Analyst with the Office the Superintendent of Bankruptcy
Canada supports this view.

[
37
]

In his letter dated June 24, 2010, Mr.
Armstrong responded to a request from Mr. Kalo as to whether any of the costs
ordered against him would be included in the bankruptcy. Mr. Armstrong stated
that he was unable to answer his question but commented: “I believe that this
fact situation as presented to me leaves argument on both sides of the issue,
and accordingly I am unwilling to offer an opinion.”    In a second letter,
dated August 13, 2010, he stated that he still could not give a concrete
response as to the status of the costs claims.

[
38
]

While Mr. Armstrong’s comments are no authority
to even support a claim that the issue is a live one, in my view there is no
issue.
Section 121(1)
of the
Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act

provides that only debts and liabilities the bankrupt owes on the date of his
assignment or that he incurred before the date of his assignment to which he
may become subject prior to his discharge are provable.  It reads:

121.
(1) All
debts and liabilities, present or future, to which the bankrupt is subject on
the day on which the bankrupt becomes bankrupt or to which the bankrupt may
become subject before the bankrupt’s discharge by reason of any obligation
incurred before the day on which the bankrupt becomes bankrupt shall be deemed
to be claims provable in proceedings under this Act.

[
39
]

In
Chaloux v.
Kingston Fairways Golf Course
2004 CanLII 25162 (ON SC)
, [2004] O.J. No.
336 (QL) Belch J. of the Ontario Court of Justice refused to consider an order
of costs, not yet made, with respect to an action commenced before the
plaintiff’s assignment in bankruptcy, to be extinquished by the bankruptcy.  In
coming to that decision, the judge referred to an English
case,
Glenister v. Rowe,
[1999] E.W.J.
No. 2585 (C.A.), and after
comparing the English legislation to s. 121(1) of the B.I.A., Belch J. stated:

31
I do not accept that an award of
costs is caught by s. 121(1) of the Act.

32
Given the provisions are similar, I
find the English decision very persuasive.

33
Also, while that case dealt with
the costs of an appeal, trial costs were also mentioned. Reading from paragraph
32(3)

... it is accepted that before an order is made there is no
present liability to pay. Nor can there be a future liability; there is no
certainty that the court will exercise its discretion to make such an order.
If, as some of the authorities hold, a contingent liability must arise out of
an existing or underlying liability, no such liability can exist simply by
reason of a claim for costs made in a writ ... or notice of appeal ...
[emphasis mine]

And continuing at paragraph 32(4)

... the discretionary nature of the court's power to order costs
indicates that there is no liability, contingent or otherwise, in the absence
of a court order ... it is necessary to identify something agreed or some act
done by Mr. Glenister to give rise to a liability on his part ... when Mr.
Glenister issued his summons ... those acts ... they are, in my view, no more
than notifications by him to the opposing party, Mrs. Rowe, that in certain events,
usually the success of the proceedings, a request will be made to the court to
make an order for costs. Such notification of a claim cannot, ... involve any
commitment by Mr. Glenister to a course of action which will necessarily and
ultimately lead to the actual order for costs against him ...

And reading from paragraph 33 of the decision of Lord Justice
Thorpe,

... the element of contingency is certainly satisfied but in my
judgment, the element of liability is not. The future exercise of the court's
discretion might eliminate that risk of liability. Equally it might elevate the
risk of liability into an actual liability, either present, in diem, or subject
to taxation. This essential distinction between incurring a liability and
exposing oneself to the risk of liability should not be undermined.

[
40
]

In
Strini v.
Mihalicz
,
2006 ABQB 912
,[2006] A.J. No. 1621
(QL), Kenny J of the Alberta Court of Queen’s Bench held that a cost award she
was making against a discharged bankrupt with respect to litigation that
commenced prior to the assignment in bankruptcy was not provable in
bankruptcy.  She referred to
Chaloux

supra
and
Glenister

and stated:

27
The essence of the
ruling of the English Court of Appeal is that a claim for costs is purely
discretionary and comes into existence only when the court makes the order. At
the time of bankruptcy there was merely a risk of costs being awarded at a
future date. There was no contingent provable liability. Therefore, the Court
of Appeal ruled that the costs order did not fall within the bankruptcy.

28
Applying
Glenister
the court,
in
Chaloux v. Kingston Fairways Golf
Course

(2004)
2004 CanLII 25162 (ON SC)
,
48 C.B.R. (4th) 237
(Ont. S.C.J.)
awarded costs against an
undischarged bankrupt. Here the plaintiff was seeking damages for assault. The
action did not proceed. The plaintiff declared bankruptcy. After the
plaintiff's discharge from bankruptcy, the defendant sought costs. Such were
awarded based on the reasoning in
Glenister.

29
I adopt the
reasoning in
Glenister
.
Costs are a completely discretionary remedy. There is no obligation until there
is an order for payment. I am therefore satisfied that any costs I might award
would not be provable in bankruptcy and are therefore not released by the
discharge granted.

In my view, the costs
to Law Society were not extinguished by his bankruptcy and remain outstanding.  The applicant, who was qualified as a lawyer in Israel, ought at
this point in time to have realized the bankruptcy is no excuse for non-payment
of the costs.

Other Factors

[
41
]

Rule 56.01 gives the court a very broad
discretion with respect to security for costs.  In determining whether it is
“just” to order security for
costs, the jurisprudence has discussed factors in addition to those set out in
the rule.

[
42
]

In
Debono v. Smith
,
1989 CanLII 7278 (MB QB)
, [1989] M.J. No. 550 (Q.B.) (QL) Hanssen J. commented:

Rule 56 gives the court a very broad discretion not
only to decide whether
security
for costs
should be ordered, but also to determine the amount and form of
the security ... .

Factors, in addition to those set out in Rule 56.01,
which the court may take into consideration in exercising its discretion,
include:

a)  the apparent merits of the Plaintiff's case;

b)  the amount of costs the Defendants have
already incurred in defending the action;

c)  the amount of the costs that might be
assessed against the Plaintiff, if the Plaintiff is unsuccessful;

d)  whether there is reason to believe the
Plaintiff has insufficient assets to satisfy a judgment for costs;

e)  whether the Plaintiff has any assets in
Manitoba that would be available to satisfy a judgment for costs;

f)  whether the Plaintiff resides or carries on
business in a reciprocating state under The
Reciprocal Enforcement of Judgments
Act, R.S.M. 1987, c.J20
;

g)  whether the Plaintiff has any assets in a
reciprocating state that would be available to satisfy a judgment for costs;

h)  whether there is reason to believe the
Plaintiff might attempt to avoid paying a judgment for costs;

i)  whether there is reason to believe an order
for
security for costs might have
the effect of preventing a Plaintiff from proceeding with a meritorious claim;

j)  the manner in which the proceedings have been
conducted by the parties.

[
43
]

The Manitoba Court of Appeal in
Franck v.
Webster
,
[1998] M.J. No. 246 (QL)
commented that the list in
DeBono v. Smith
was a
"handy guide" but the enumerated factors are "not fixed judicial
add-ons”  to the grounds set out in the rule:

30   One other observation needs to be made in light
of the heavy reliance placed by the motions court judge on the
"checklist" set forth
in
DeBono v. Smith
. While the enumerated
factors suggested
in
DeBono
are a handy guide, they should not be taken as an
exhaustive list to be routinely considered in every case. They are not fixed
judicial add-ons to the enumerated grounds set forth in Rule 56.01. Not all of
the examples listed
in
DeBono
will be relevant or appropriate in every case. A
good example is this case, where it would not have been proper to take into
account "the apparent merits of the plaintiff's case," one of the
suggested factors enumerated
in
DeBono
.

[
44
]

The Court of Appeal stated that it is
"crucial that each case be looked at on its own merits to determine
whether ‘in the particular circumstances’ it is ‘just’ to order
security for costs
”.
The court warned against
using the rule as a device to "get rid" of an action seen to be of
questionable merit. The appropriate process in that circumstance is a motion
for summary judgment. The court commented:

32   It is also essential, despite the discretion given
under Rule 56, that judges considering an application for
security for costs exercise caution to ensure that the
rule is being used for the purpose for which it was intended. Queen's Bench
Rule 20 provides a summary mechanism for plaintiffs and defendants to move for
judgment if it is thought that a claim or defence lacks merit. Where there is
concern about delay on the part of a plaintiff, Rule 24 enables a defendant to
make a motion for dismissal of the action. There is now no justification, if
there ever was one, to use the rule for
security for costs as a shortcut device to "get rid
of" an action perceived to be of dubious merit, or where there has been
undue delay on the part of the plaintiff. An order for
security for costs should only be granted where it is
essential to do so, in the interests of justice, to provide defendants with
some protection for their potential costs. An example would be where a
plaintiff, though resident in Manitoba, has virtually all his assets located in
an off-shore jurisdiction.

45

,

2004 MBQB 204
, [2004] M.J. No. 350 (QL), impecuniosity is a “double-edged sword”. It is one of the factors,
as set out in
Debono
, that the court can consider justifies an
order for security for costs, but it is also a factor militating against an
order.  Indeed, as a general rule the court does not order an impecunious
plaintiff to pay security for costs. The fundamental question is really,
notwithstanding the plaintiff’s impecuniosity, whether
there are other factors which make such an order just.

47
]

In

Laboratory Services Inc
.,
2006 MBCA 85
, [2006] M.J. No 344, (QL) Scott

It is clear that a financially disadvantaged litigant

Franck
at para. 32 and
Silver v. Co-operators General
Insurance Co.
,
[2002] N.S.J. No. 8
,
2002 NSCA 6
.
The plaintiff alleges that she is
"experiencing an extreme financial crisis" due to being unemployed

6

substantial security for costs should be granted on the one hand, and on the
other that plaintiff's
[
sic
]

with a case that does not
clearly lack merit not be deprived of their day in court solely due to their
impecuniosity, I have concluded, in the interests of justice, that it is
"just" to provide Westman with some modest measure of financial
security for their potential costs. I would fix the amount at $ 2,000 all
inclusive.

Franck Estate v. Webster et al
.,

1998 CanLII 6168 (MB CA)

129 Man.R. (2d) 87

at para.
32
).

10

Moss Estate (Bankrupt),
